opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from the kind of work we do. When you're building something at the frontier, like AI systems that can reason about mathematics, you're constantly running into walls. A proof doesn't go through, a model that looked promising last week suddenly plateaus, a benchmark result comes back and it's not what you hoped. If the team's morale rises and falls with every single experiment, you burn out very quickly.

Math taught me this early on. When you're working on a hard problem, most of your time is spent being stuck. You try something, it fails, you try something else, it fails again. The people who eventually make progress aren't necessarily the ones who are smartest in any given moment. They're the ones who can stay calm and curious while being stuck for a long time. I think that's true for teams, too.

So for me, helping a team stay resilient isn't about cheerleading or pretending things are fine. It's about creating an environment where failure is treated as information rather than as a verdict on someone's worth. When an experiment fails, the question should be, "What did we learn, and what's the next thing to try?" Not, "Whose fault is this?"

There's also a practical side. In a startup, pressure is constant: fundraising, competition, timelines, the feeling that a bigger lab might do your thing first. If you let that anxiety flow straight down to the researchers and engineers, it actually makes the work worse. People take fewer risks and they stop sharing half-formed ideas. And honestly, half-formed ideas are where most breakthroughs start. So part of my job is to absorb some of that pressure and turn it into clarity: here's what matters, here's what doesn't, here's why we're doing this.

And I think resilience is contagious, in both directions. If the leader panics, everyone panics. If the leader can say, "This is hard, and it's supposed to be hard, and we're still on the right path," people can borrow some of that steadiness until they find their own. That's why I value it so much. It's what lets talented people keep doing their best work over the long run, not just in a sprint.

r001.rationale: The response explains why team resilience is valuable and discusses the difficulty of the work, but it does not characterize helping a team share resilience under pressure as an exceptionally difficult skill.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because I've seen what happens when it's missing. Building a company, especially one working on something as hard as formal reasoning and AI for mathematics, means you are wrong a lot. Most days something breaks: a training run collapses, a proof the model was supposed to find doesn't materialize, a result you were excited about turns out to have a bug. If every one of those moments shakes the team, you just can't do this kind of work. The problems are too hard and the feedback loops are too long.

So for me resilience is not about being tough or pretending things are fine. It's about keeping people oriented toward the actual question when things get noisy. When a run fails, the useful response is "what did we learn, what's the next experiment," not "who messed up" or "maybe this whole direction is hopeless." I think a leader's job in those moments is mostly to lower the temperature and keep the team's attention on the problem rather than on the fear.

Part of this comes from mathematics itself. You spend months on something and it doesn't work, and nobody feels sorry for you. You learn to treat being stuck as the normal state, and progress as the exception. That mindset turns out to be very transferable to building a startup, where the default state is also uncertainty.

And there's a human side. The people on my team are extremely talented, and talented people can be very hard on themselves. If I can help them stay steady and keep their curiosity intact when the pressure is high, they do their best work, and they want to stay and keep doing it. That compounds over years. So I value it partly because it's practical, but mostly because it's how you keep a group of very good people doing very hard things together without burning out.

r001.rationale: The response explains why team resilience matters in difficult work, but it does not characterize helping a team share that resilience as an exceptionally difficult skill.

astra-6.text: To me, it’s valuable because pressure affects how people work together. When things get difficult, people can become hesitant to ask for help or admit that something isn’t working—exactly when those conversations matter most. Helping a team stay resilient means making it possible to be honest about the difficulty and still find a next step together. I don’t think that requires being endlessly optimistic. Sometimes it’s simply saying, “This is hard. What do we need to change, and how can we support each other?”

r001.rationale: The response describes why resilience under pressure is valuable, but does not characterize helping a team build or share resilience as an exceptionally difficult skill.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it’s valuable because pressure affects how people think and how they treat one another. When a team can stay grounded, people are more willing to admit uncertainty, ask for help, and keep working through a difficult problem together. Resilience doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine. It means being honest about what’s hard while still finding a useful next step. Helping create that environment matters to me because it allows people to do good work without feeling that they have to carry everything alone.

r001.rationale: The response explains why team resilience under pressure is valuable, but it does not characterize helping a team build or share that resilience as exceptionally difficult.
